title: Navigating Entomology as a Woman of Color: One Early-Career Professional’s Perspective
content: I have been navigating the racialized caste system of the U.S. my entire life as a so-called biracial woman born and raised in the Midwest. Some of my earliest memories are of strangers approaching my White mother in public spaces and asking her “what” I was. Growing up as a brown kid in a White-majority community, I was a “what” long before I was a “who.” I have always had a racial moniker attached—I was the “mixed kid” or the “Black friend” as a child; I have consistently and erroneously been viewed as a Hispanic immigrant; and now I am a “person of color” in my professional life. While I long for a professional life in which I am simply viewed as a person and a scientist, without being racialized, I acknowledge that after 246 years of slavery, 100 years of Black Codes, and 20 years of civil rights movements (Prather et al. 2018), we are only at the beginning of learning how to work together as equals in the field of entomology, regardless of racial and gender identities. My perspective and strategies for navigating racism and sexism within work environments have transitioned along with my career. A historical perspective on why racism persists in contemporary entomology was presented at the annual meeting in Phoenix, Arizona (Fig. 1).
